en: Petavatthu, Cūḷavagga 8. The Second Story of the Gamekeeper Who Became a Ghost [The Buddha said: "Once upon a time, monks, there was a gamekeeper who lived by hunting deer. He would kill many deer with arrows and sell their meat for a living. One day, while he was wandering about, he saw a doe carrying her fawn. Seeing her, he shot an arrow at her. The arrow struck the mother doe, but it passed through her and struck the fawn; the arrow then emerged from the other side of the fawn’s body. The fawn, pierced by the arrow, fell to the ground and died. The mother doe, seeing her son dead, wept and lamented: ‘Alas, my son! Alas, my son! Then, monks, that gamekeeper, having committed that evil deed, was reborn in the state of a hungry ghost (petā). After passing away from there, he was reborn in hell. Having experienced the suffering in hell, he was reborn here among humans as a poor man. He went to a certain village to beg for alms. There, he saw a woman who was a devoted lay follower (upāsikā) who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem and observed the five precepts. She was giving alms to a monk. Seeing this, the ghost thought: ‘If only she would give me some food. Then, monks, that woman, out of compassion, took a portion of rice from her own bowl and gave it to the ghost. Because of that gift, the ghost was released from that state of suffering. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall practice generosity and refrain from taking life. This is how you should train yourselves. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [End of] The Second Story of the Gamekeeper Who Became a Ghost.
In a gabled chamber and a palace,
upon a couch spread with woolen blankets,
accompanied by the fivefold musical ensemble—
You delight in being well-praised.
Then, at the end of that night,
as the sun rises;
Cast away in the charnel ground,
you undergo much suffering.
What indeed [have you done] by body or by speech?
An evil deed was committed with the mind;
as the result of what karma do you undergo this suffering?
“In the delightful city of Rājagaha,
on the charming Giribbaja mountain,
I was formerly a deer-hunter.”
A hunter, unrestrained in his sword and meat,
had a companion who was kind-hearted—
a faithful lay follower.
His attendant monk was a disciple of Gotama;
out of compassion for me, he too—
He restrained him again and again:
"Do not commit an evil deed;
do not, my dear, go to a state of misery."
"If you desire happiness after passing away,
refrain from killing living beings and from lack of restraint.
Having heard his words, I—
Though he desired my happiness and was compassionate for my welfare,
I, lacking wisdom and long delighted in evil,
did not follow his complete instruction.
Thus, out of compassion, the one of vast wisdom established me again in self-restraint, saying:
"If you kill living beings during the day,"
"Then let there be restraint for you by night.
"By day I have killed living beings,
but by night I am abstinent and self-controlled."
At night I enjoy my pleasures,
but by day I am devoured, fallen into misfortune.
Of that wholesome deed...
I experience this non-human state at night;
by day, dogs, being thwarted,
run about from all sides seeking to devour me.
And those who are constantly devoted, firmly applied to the teaching of the Sugata—
I consider them to have attained only the Deathless.
“They attain the unconditioned state.
This is the eighth story, the second concerning the deer-hunter peta.
